lead: Put N objects into k boxes. If N is larger than k, at least one box must hold more than one object. That is the pigeonhole principle. It exists to turn a counting fact into a guarantee: you do not find which box, only that one box must be full enough. The generalized form gives the exact minimum: some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects. It is used in scheduling, hashing, error detection, and quick proofs about repeated colours, months or subset sums. Some syllabi spell it 'pigeon hole principle'.
prereq: You need: 3.1 counting rules and proof by contradiction from Unit 1, Proof methods: direct, indirect and by contradiction.

blocks.text: Call the containers boxes and the items objects. Every object goes into exactly one box. If there are N objects and k boxes and N > k, then some box contains at least two objects. The reason is a maximum count: if every box had at most one object, the total would be at most k. But N > k, so all N objects cannot fit.
N > k ⇒ some box has at least 2 objects
blocks.where: N is the number of objects; k is the number of boxes; ⇒ means implies.

blocks.text: This is a proof by contradiction. Assume every box holds at most one object. The largest possible total is k, which is smaller than N. Contradiction. The same idea can also be written as a contrapositive argument.
Example: 13 people and 12 birth months. Since 13 > 12, two people share a birth month. The principle does not say January. It says some month. This is why the result is a guarantee, not a prediction.

The simple form counts a repeat of 2. The generalized form gives the exact minimum for any repeat count. Put N objects into k boxes. Some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects. Here ⌈x⌉ is the ceiling of x: the smallest integer greater than or equal to x.

blocks.where: N is the number of objects; k is the number of boxes; ⌊ ⌋ rounds down to an integer; ⌈ ⌉ rounds up to an integer.

blocks.text: The formula uses integer arithmetic. It is exact, not an estimate. If N = 7 and k = 3, then ⌈7/3⌉ = ⌈2.333...⌉ = 3. So 7 socks in 3 colours force 3 socks of one colour. With 6 socks, the split 2, 2, 2 is possible, so 6 is not enough.
N ≥ k(r − 1) + 1 ⇒ some box has at least r objects
blocks.where: N is the number of objects; k is the number of boxes; r is the target count in one box; the smallest such N is k(r − 1) + 1.

blocks.text: To force r objects in some box, take k(r − 1) + 1 objects. One fewer gives k(r − 1) objects, which can be split as r − 1 in every box. The bound is tight: it cannot be lowered. The principle gives a lower bound on the fullest box, not an exact count of every box; exact counts need 3.4.

sections.h3: Proof by contradiction and a subset pattern

blocks.text: Prove the generalized form by contradiction. Let m = ⌈N/k⌉. Suppose every box holds at most m − 1 objects. The total number of objects is at most k(m − 1). By the definition of ceiling, m − 1 < N/k, so k(m − 1) < N. The total would be less than N, but all N objects are placed. Contradiction. Therefore some box holds at least m objects.
The same argument proves the r-form. If every box had at most r − 1 objects, the total would be at most k(r − 1). Choosing N = k(r − 1) + 1 makes this total less than N, a contradiction.

Subset example. Choose any 6 distinct integers from 1 to 10. Pair the numbers as {1, 10}, {2, 9}, {3, 8}, {4, 7}, {5, 6}. There are 5 pairs, and each pair sums to 11. Six chosen numbers go into 5 pairs, so two chosen numbers fall in the same pair. Those two sum to 11. The principle guarantees such a pair exists; it does not say which pair.

figure.caption: Three colour boxes hold 3, 2 and 2 socks. The first box reaches 3, so 7 socks force three of one colour; 6 socks could split as 2, 2, 2.

spec.title: 7 socks into 3 colours
spec.aria: Three colour boxes hold 3, 2 and 2 socks, so one box reaches 3.

examples.question: A drawer has red, blue and green socks. In the dark, how many socks must you take to guarantee at least three socks of one colour? Show that one fewer sock does not guarantee this.
steps: Boxes are the 3 colours: red, blue and green. Objects are the socks drawn.
The target repeat count is r = 3.
Use the r-form: smallest N = k(r − 1) + 1 with k = 3 and r = 3.
With 6 socks, the split 2 red, 2 blue, 2 green has no colour reaching 3, so 6 socks are not enough.
With 7 socks, ⌈7/3⌉ = 3, so some colour has at least 3 socks.
examples.answer: Answer: 7 socks; with 7 socks some colour has at least 3 socks.
examples.check:
k = 3
r = 3
min_socks = k * (r - 1) + 1
forced = (min_socks + k - 1) // k
print(min_socks)
print(forced)

traps: Using floor instead of ceiling: floor(7/3) = 2, but 7 socks in 3 colours force 3, because 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 is the largest total with no colour reaching 3.
Claiming a named box, colour or month must reach the bound. The principle guarantees only that some box does.
Confusing 'at least r' with 'exactly r'. The fullest box may hold r + 1 or more.
Writing N/k with integer division. Use the ceiling formula; if N/k is an integer, the bound is N/k, not N/k + 1.
Forgetting the exact condition for r: N must be k(r − 1) + 1 or more, not k·r.

quiz.q: State the generalized pigeonhole principle for N objects in k boxes.
quiz.a: Some box contains at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects, where ⌈·⌉ is the ceiling.

quiz.q: Why is floor(N/k) the wrong bound? Use N = 7, k = 3.
quiz.a: floor(7/3) = 2, but 6 socks can be 2 per colour; the 7th forces a third sock in some colour, so the guarantee is ⌈7/3⌉ = 3. Floor undercounts.

quiz.q: 25 students are put into 6 project groups. What is the smallest guaranteed size of the largest group?
quiz.a: ⌈25/6⌉ = ⌈4.166...⌉ = 5. Some group has at least 5 students.

quiz.q: How many people guarantee that 4 share a birth month? Use 12 months.
quiz.a: k = 12, r = 4. N = 12(4 − 1) + 1 = 37. With 36 people, 3 per month is possible.

quiz.q: Show that any 6 distinct integers from 1 to 10 contain two that sum to 11.
quiz.a: Use 5 pairs {1, 10}, {2, 9}, {3, 8}, {4, 7}, {5, 6}. Six integers into 5 pairs force two in one pair; that pair sums to 11.

quiz.q: A student says the principle proves box 3 has at least 2 objects. Is that valid?
quiz.a: No. The principle proves at least one box has at least 2 objects. It does not name box 3.

quiz.q: A hash table has 9 buckets and 100 keys. What is the minimum possible maximum bucket size? Justify.
quiz.a: Some bucket has at least ⌈100/9⌉ = 12 keys. A size of 12 is also achievable: eight buckets hold 11 keys and one holds 12, giving 8 × 11 + 12 = 100. So the minimum possible maximum bucket size is exactly 12.

beyond: Not for the exam. The pigeonhole idea grows into Ramsey theory, where a large enough structure forces a regular substructure. In computing, it explains why hash tables need load factors and why collisions are unavoidable when keys exceed buckets. A probabilistic technique called the probabilistic method can show that some assignment exists by proving a random assignment has positive probability of being good. It is not a form of the pigeonhole principle. Search for 'pigeonhole principle Ramsey theory' and 'hash table load factor' to go further.
